0158               
0159               ; While we don't mean to USE the console ROM, for interrupts we
0160               ; are forced to interface with some of it. We need these addresses
0161               ; to minimize what it does so we can maximize our use of scratchpad.
0162               ; While I'd like to use the cassette hook - requires only 10 instructions
0163               ; and only uses 6 words of scratchpad, we can't here because it
0164               ; loses the return address, meaning you can only use it if you
0165               ; know where your LIMI 2 is and interrupts are otherwise disabled. So
0166               ; we have to use the longer but more standard interrupt hook, which also
0167               ; reads VDP status for us (no choice).
0168               
0169      8379     intcnt              equ >8379   ; interrupt counter byte, adds 1 (from GPLWS r14) every frame
0170      837B     vdp_status          equ >837B   ; VDP status byte mirror
0171      83C2     intwsr1             equ >83c2   ; INT WS R1  - interrupt control flags - must be >8000
0172      83C4     intwsr2             equ >83c4   ; INT WS R2  - address of user interrupt routine (point to int_handler)
0173      83D6     intwsr11            equ >83d6   ; screen timeout counter - must be odd (init to 1, is inct every frame)
0174      83DA     intwsr13            equ >83da   ; INT WS R13 - used for interrupt call (word)
0175      83DC     intwsr14            equ >83dc   ; INT WS R14 - used for interrupt call (word)
0176      83DE     intwsr15            equ >83de   ; INT WS R15 - used for interrupt call (word)
0177      83F6     gplwsr11            equ >83f6   ; GPL WS R11 - return address to interrupt ROM (not used, but overwritten each int)
0178      83F8     gplwsr12            equ >83f8   ; GPL WS R12 - used for cassette test and interrupt hook test (zeroed each int)
0179      83FA     gplwsr13            equ >83fa   ; GPL WS R13 - used in my interrupt handler
0180      83FC     gplwsr14            equ >83fc   ; GPL WS R14 - flags used to detect cassette - must be >0108 (or at least >0020 clear)
0181      83FE     gplwsr15            equ >83fe   ; GPL WS R15 - base address of VDP for status read - must be >8C02

0470               ; Load sprite definitions: Sprite number in R4, CPU data in R0, count of sprites in R5 (MSB)
0471               ; Original: pointer = sprite number, temp = CPU address, a = number sprites
0472               ; Note: sprites are all expected to be double-size 16x16, 32 bytes each, so sprite char 1 is character 4
0473               ; Sprite pattern table at >3800

     A1E4 3800

     A1F6 0002

0545               ; SGN R0 - return 1, -1 or 0 as 16 bit
0546               _sgn16
0547 A260 C000  18     mov r0,r0       ; check for zero
0548 A262 1306  14     jeq !1          ; if yes, we're done
0549 A264 0240  22     andi r0,>8000   ; check for negative
     A266 8000     
0550 A268 1302  14     jeq !2          ; was not
0551 A26A 0700  14     seto r0         ; was negative, make it -1
0552 A26C 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0553               !2
0554 A26E 0580  14     inc r0          ; we know it was zero, and we want 1
0555               !1
0556 A270 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0557               
0558               ; 16-bit signed modulo. R1 % R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0559               ; original was stack%stack=YYAA
0560               ; Remainder is negative if the dividend was negative
0561               _mod16s
0562 A272 04C0  14     clr r0          ; make dividend 32-bit
0563 A274 C082  18     mov r2,r2       ; check divisor for zero
0564 A276 130A  14     jeq !1
0565 A278 0742  18     abs r2          ; make sure divisor is positive
0566 A27A C041  18     mov r1,r1       ; check sign of dividend
0567 A27C 1505  14     jgt !2          ; go do the faster positive version
0568               
0569 A27E 0741  18     abs r1          ; was negative, make it positive
0570 A280 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0571 A282 0501  14     neg r1          ; make remainder negative
0572 A284 C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0573 A286 045B  20     b *r11
0574               
0575               !2
0576 A288 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0577 A28A C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0578               !1
0579 A28C 045B  20     b *r11
0580               
0581               ; 16-bit signed divide. R1 / R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0582               ; original was stack/stack=YYAA
0583               ; Remainder is negative if the signs differ
0584               _div16s

0587 A292 1308  14     jeq !1          ;

     A29E 8000

0832               
0833               ; this is where interrupts happen every frame
0834               ; Unlike a normal TI application, this one runs with interrupts ON,
0835               ; so all operations need to be sure to protect VDP address with LIMI 0,
0836               ; as well as any operations that might need to manipulate data managed
0837               ; by this interrupt. We enter via the normal user hook, so WP is on
0838               ; GPLWS, interrupts are off, and the VDP is already reset and status
0839               ; stashed on vdp_status (>837b). Our return address to the ROM is in
0840               ; r11, but we are NOT going to use it so that we don't need to reserve
0841               ; r8 for whatever nonsense it does. That means we need to load intws
0842               ; and RTWP ourselves at the end. We are on our own workspace so we
0843               ; don't have to worry about the main app's workspace.
0844               int_handler
0845               ; first copy the sprite table
0846 A48E 02E0  18     lwpi myintwp        ; separate safe workspace
     A490 8320     
0847               
0849 A492 C820  46     mov @>7ffe,@saved_bank  ; save bank switch page
     A494 7FFE     
     A496 8372     
0851               
0852 A498 020B  20     li r11,>005b        ; >1b00 with the write bit added, and byte flipped
     A49A 005B     
0853 A49C D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; SAL address
     A49E 8C02     
0854 A4A0 06CB  14     swpb r11
0855 A4A2 D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; going to copy the sprite table to VDP
     A4A4 8C02     
0856               
0857 A4A6 D2E0  30     movb @mode,r11
     A4A8 834E

1315                   ;
1316                   ; Converts note to frequency.
1317                   ; Input
1318                   ;   A = Instrument         (r0 - msb)
1319                   ;   X = Instrument counter (r1 - msb)
1320                   ;   Y = Note (1-62)        (r2 - msb)
1321                   ; Output
1322                   ;   YA = Frequency. (r0 - word)
1323                   ;   X = Volume.     (r1 - msb)
1324                   ;
1325               music_note2freq
1326 A8EA 0982  32     srl r2,8                ; make int so they can be indexes
1327 A8EC 0A12  18     sla r2,1                ; make word index
1328 A8EE 0981  32     srl r1,8                ; just byte index here
1329 A8F0 06C0  14     swpb r0
1330 A8F2 D001  18     movb r1,r0              ; conveniently we now know it's >00 so we can clear out r0's LSB for easier tests
1331 A8F4 06C0  14     swpb r0
1332

     A8F8 4000

1335 A8FC 1326  14     jeq music_clarinet
1336 A8FE 0280  22     ci r0,>8000
     A900 8000     
1337 A902 13D2  14     jeq music_flute

1928               
1929               ; The stack is simulated using R10. It's not used in
1930               ; these functions but the compiled code will need it.
1931               ; To push: dect r10, mov r0,*r10
1932               ; To pop:  mov *r10+,r0
1933               ; However, for JSR a function is helpful - call this like:
1934               ; bl @jsr
1935               ; data <function_address>
1936               jsr
1937 AE2A C3BB  30     mov *r11+,r14       ; get the jump address
1938 AE2C 064A  14     dect r10            ; make room on stack
1939 AE2E C68B  30     mov r11,*r10        ; save return address
1940 AE30 069E  24     bl *r14             ; new subroutine call, we can come back here
1941 AE32 C2FA  30     mov *r10+,r11       ; get real return off stack - warning, all basic functions do this inline rather than return
1942 AE34 045B  20     b *r11              ; back to caller

     AE44 8802     
     AE46 837B

1984               ;;; CVBasic code starts here
1985               	; 	' ==========================================================================
1986               	; 	' KEYSTONE KAPERS -- CVBasic, dual target TI-99/4A + ColecoVision.
1987               	; 	'
1988               	; 	' Garry Kitchen's 1983 Activision game. See DESIGN.md; 0 records the
1989               	; 	' research and the four places the sources disagree.
1990               	; 	'
1991               	; 	' Fifty seconds to run Harry Hooligan down inside a department store eight
1992               	; 	' screens wide and four levels tall, before he reaches the roof.
1993               	; 	'
1994               	; 	' THE THREE DECISIONS THIS FILE IS BUILT ON, all from DESIGN.md:
1995               	; 	'
1996               	; 	'   * THE VIEW FLIPS, IT DOES NOT SCROLL. Eight discrete screens; crossing
1997               	; 	'     an edge blits the next one. The per-frame budget never pays for the
1998               	; 	'     store at all -- RallyX repaints 576 chars every camera cell and had
1999               	; 	'     to have all its movement rewritten to survive that.
2000               	; 	'   * A SCREEN IS EXACTLY 256 PX, so an actor's x within its screen is one
2001               	; 	'     unsigned byte. No 16-bit world coordinate exists in this program.
2002               	; 	'   * ZERO PER-FRAME VDP READS. An actor's floor is an index into flry(),
2003               	; 	'     never a question asked of the screen, so the Ms. Pac-Man trap
2004               	; 	'     (actors x per-actor search) is absent by construction.
2005               	; 	'
2006               	; 	' The rules that shaped the code, all from CLAUDE.md 3A, because every one
2007               	; 	' of them fails SILENTLY:
2008               	; 	'
2009               	; 	'   * A plain variable is 8-BIT and a CONST over 255 TRUNCATES. Every
2010               	; 	'     name-table offset past row 7 is a #var or a bare literal.
2011               	; 	'   * Every #var comparison is UNSIGNED.
2012               	; 	'   * `<cmp> AND <cmp>` is miscompiled by the 9900 backend. Nested IFs.
2013               	; 	'   * A sprite at y=208 TERMINATES the sprite list. Hidden sprites go 209.
2014               	; 	'   * A GOSUB left by GOTO never pops. Death, catch and escape are STATES
2015               	; 	'     set in a routine and acted on at the top of the main loop.
2016               	; 	'   * MPY clobbers r0. Nothing here multiplies into an index -- the tables
2017               	; 	'     tsrc()/bdst()/lv8() exist precisely so that no multiply is needed on
2018               	; 	'     a path that reads the result back.
2019               	; 	' ==========================================================================
2020               	;
2021               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- BANKING
2022               	; 	' THE ART AND THE STORE MAP LIVE IN ROM BANK 1 ON THE TI. The fixed area
2023               	; 	' is 24,336 bytes -- three 8,112-byte loader pages -- and unbanked this
2024               	; 	' program filled 24,304 of them, so there was no room left for anything at
2025               	; 	' all. `linkticart` does not warn when you exceed it; it silently discards
2026               	; 	' the top of the image, and what goes missing is whatever sits nearest the
2027               	; 	' end, usually a DATA block rather than code. Nothing errors.
2028               	; 	'
2029               	; 	' WHAT IS SAFE TO BANK. Everything moved here is read at SETUP (the
2030               	; 	' DEFINE CHAR / DEFINE SPRITE calls) or on a screen crossing (the template
2031               	; 	' blit and the escalator's phase tables) -- and, because there is exactly
2032               	; 	' ONE data bank and it is selected ONCE at startup and never switched, it
2033               	; 	' stays mapped for the life of the program. The rule in CLAUDE.md 3A is
2034               	; 	' about SWITCHING inside a frame or under the vblank ISR; with a single
2035               	; 	' permanently-selected bank there is no switch to miss. A missed
2036               	; 	' BANK SELECT would return bytes from the wrong page with no error at
2037               	; 	' build or run time, which is why there is only one and it is set before
2038               	; 	' anything reads from it.
2039               	; 	'
2040               	; 	' BANK ROM 128 sizes ColecoVision's Megacart mapper, NOT the TI cart --
2041               	; 	' that comes from how many bank files the assembler emits -- and it is
2042               	; 	' one of only four values the compiler accepts (128/256/512/1024).
2043               	; 	' The whole thing is gated on TI994A: the Coleco build is Z80 and roughly
2044               	; 	' half the size, so it neither needs banking nor wants to become a
2045               	; 	' Megacart image.
2046               	; 	#if TI994A
2047               	; 	BANK ROM 128
2048               	; 	#endif
2049               	; 	#if NES
2050               	; 	' 240 ON THE NES, AND THIS WAS THE FLICKER. There is no sprite-list
2051               	; 	' terminator on that machine -- y is simply a row -- so 209 is a VISIBLE
2052               	; 	' one, and every "hidden" sprite was being drawn in a heap near the bottom
2053               	; 	' of the screen with pattern 0, which is Kelly's hat. Two dozen of them on

2063               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------------- geometry
2064               	; 	' A band is 5 rows: 4 rows of air (32 px) over one floor slab. Standing
2065               	; 	' Kelly is 16 px, so headroom is 16 px and the jump apex is 14 -- two
2066               	; 	' short of the ceiling, because an arc that bonks is silently truncated.
2067               	; 	' 4 px/frame = 240 px/s. At 2 it was not merely sluggish, it was
2068               	; 	' ARITHMETICALLY TOO SLOW: the climb is three traverses = 6,144 px, which
2069               	; 	' at 2 px/frame is 51 seconds of pure running against a 50-second clock,
2070               	; 	' before a single obstacle, escalator ride or catch. At 3 it is 34 s --
2071               	; 	' and 34 s was still wrong, for a reason a per-actor speed check cannot
2072               	; 	' see: HARRY'S CLIMB IS ALSO 34 s (DESIGN.md 4a). Kelly being 1.5x faster
2073               	; 	' bought nothing, because Harry's route is two thirds the length of
2074               	; 	' Kelly's -- he spawns beside floor 2's escalator and effectively skips a
2075               	; 	' traverse. A chase resolves on PATH / SPEED, not on speed, and the two
2076               	; 	' quotients were equal, so pursuit on foot could never close. At 4 the
2077               	; 	' climb is 25 s against Harry's 45, and the elevator buys back more.
2078               	; 	CONST WALKSP = 4		' px per PASS -- the old unit, kept only for

2082               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS OF A PIXEL PER FRAME, which is what he actually walks by.
2083               	; 	'
2084               	; 	' HIS OLD BEST-CASE SPEED, MADE CONSTANT -- not his old average. WALKSP was
2085               	; 	' 4 px per loop PASS, so what he actually did depended on the screen: 104 px/s
2086               	; 	' on a light one at 26 passes/s, 80 px/s on the lift and escalator screens at
2087               	; 	' 20. Matching the MEASURED AVERAGE of 23.8 passes/s gave 95.6 px/s (102/64),
2088               	; 	' which is the same average and an 8% loss on exactly the screens a chase
2089               	; 	' spends most of its time crossing -- the crook was already per-frame and did

2091               	; 	' read as only just catching him on the last screen.
2092               	; 	'
2093               	; 	' 111/64 is 104.1 px/s: his best case, everywhere. He is now at least as fast
2094               	; 	' as he ever was on any screen rather than faster on some and slower on

2587               	; 	' TWO SECONDS BETWEEN FLOORS. `elt` counts down by `fdv`, the FRAME
2588               	; 	' delta, so this is real frames and not loop passes -- 120 of them is
2589               	; 	' 2.0 s on both 60 Hz targets, and it stays 2.0 s when the loop gets
2590               	; 	' busy. It was 45 (0.75 s), which is faster than a lift has any business
2591               	; 	' being and gave the doors barely time to read as opening.
2592               	; 	CONST ELMOVE = 120		' frames in transit between floors
2593      0078     const_ELMOVE	equ >0078
2594               	; 	' HOW FAR THE SECOND HAZARD ON A FLOOR TRAILS THE FIRST, in pixels.
2595               	; 	'
2596               	; 	' THERE ARE ONLY TWO SAFE ANSWERS. Kelly closes on an oncoming hazard at
2597               	; 	' (KWALK64 + its speed)/64 px a FRAME -- 2.53 at the slow speed, 2.92 at
2598               	; 	' the fast one -- and the jump arc holds its apex for 9 frames and is
2599               	; 	' airborne for 28. So:
2600               	; 	'
2601               	; 	'   <= 22 px   ONE JUMP CLEARS BOTH -- the pair drifts under the apex
2602               	; 	'   >= 82 px   he can LAND BETWEEN them -- a whole jump fits in the gap
2603               	; 	'
2604               	; 	' Anything in between is the dangerous middle: too far to clear together,
2605               	; 	' too close to land between. The gap shipped at 46 px west of the lift and
2606               	; 	' 70 px east of it -- 46 is inside the first window and 70 is squarely in
2607               	; 	' that middle, which is the asymmetry that got reported. It then shipped at
2608               	; 	' 20, in the first window, which is a pair taken as ONE obstacle.
2609               	; 	'
2610               	; 	' 104 IS MEASURED FROM THE ORIGINAL, not chosen. A frame-by-frame census of
2611               	; 	' a full 2600 playthrough (assets/ref2600/hazards.md) finds that two moving
2612               	; 	' hazards on one floor are NEVER closer than 108 px in our scale -- not once
2613               	; 	' in 21 levels -- and that its static radios come as close as 54. Our own
2614               	; 	' arc independently puts the land-between threshold at 82 px for a mover and
2615               	; 	' 49 for a static one, so the original sits just above both, from evidence
2616               	; 	' that knows nothing about this jump. That is the run / jump / run / jump
2617               	; 	' the reviewer described, and it is what the 20 px pair was not.
2618               	; 	'
2619               	; 	' THE PRICE IS SLOT 0's JITTER, and it is arithmetic, not a choice. `stag`
2620               	; 	' is distance from the FAR edge, so the second hazard sits GAP px nearer the
2621               	; 	' wall the player walks in through. He needs a reaction budget there
2622               	; 	' (checkspace.py's WARNPX, 120 px), and 120 + 104 = 224 of the 240 px of
2623               	; 	' placeable floor -- so the pair can only slide 16 px. Hence HAZMASK below.
2624               	; 	' That is not less faithful than what it replaces: the original places its
2625               	; 	' radios on exactly THREE fixed positions per floor, so it has no jitter at
2626               	; 	' all. assets/checkspace.py checks the gap, the entry distance and the
2627               	; 	' offset rule together, and checkspace_test.py proves it still rejects 70
2628               	; 	' and 176 -- and now 71, which only the FASTEST hazard can see.
2629               	; 	CONST HAZGAP = 104
2630      0068     const_HAZGAP	equ >0068
2631               	; 	' Slot 0's stagger mask ONCE A FLOOR CAN CARRY TWO. Before that a floor has
2632               	; 	' one hazard, the pair arithmetic above does not apply, and slot 0 keeps its
2633               	; 	' full 64 px of jitter -- which is most of the early game, where the player
2634               	; 	' meets the fewest hazards and variety is worth the most.
2635               	; 	CONST HAZMASK = 15
2636      000F     const_HAZMASK	equ >000f
2637               	; 	CONST ELDOOR = 15		' frames the doors spend part-open
2638      000F     const_ELDOOR	equ >000f
2639               	; 	CONST ELOPEN = 85		' = ELWAIT - ELDOOR, as a literal: a CONST
2640      0055     const_ELOPEN	equ >0055
2641               	; 					' built from other CONSTs is exactly the
2642               	; 					' folded-constant trap in CLAUDE.md 3A
2643               	;
2644               	; 	' escalator boarding zones, in CENTRE-x pixels
2645               	; 	' ESCALATOR BOARDING ZONES, IN PIXELS, AND THEY TRACK THE ART.
2646               	; 	' The flight is drawn as four rows of two characters stepping two columns
2647               	; 	' per row: west runs cols 1-2 (top) down to 7-8 (foot), east runs 29-30
2648               	; 	' (top) down to 23-24 (foot). These zones ARE those columns x8. When the
2649               	; 	' escalator art changed from a filled triangle to a stepped flight the
2650               	; 	' foot moved, and a boarding zone left where it was would put the player
2651               	; 	' on a staircase that is not under them -- no error, just a floor that
2652               	; 	' teleports you when you walk over an empty patch of it.
2653               	; 	' THESE ARE THE DRAWN STEPS, in screen pixels. The flight is fifteen
2654               	; 	' characters wide: its foot tread sits at x 95-103 (west) and 152-160
2655               	; 	' (east), its head tread at 23-31 and 224-232. An actor rides between
2656               	; 	' those, so the numbers here are the ART's, and moving the art without
2657               	; 	' moving them puts the rider beside the escalator rather than on it.
2658               	; 	' THE RIDER STANDS ON A STEP, and everything about the ride follows from
2659               	; 	' WHICH ONE. The staircase is a straight line -- a step 4 px higher is 8
2660               	; 	' px further along it -- so one number, the step's height above the floor
2661               	; 	' being left, fixes both the rider's x and the rest of the ride:
2662               	; 	'
2663               	; 	'     west  klx = 99 - 2*height        east  klx = 140 + 2*height
2664               	; 	'
2665               	; 	' The bottom step is 4 px up, so a rider walking on boards at klx = 91
2666               	; 	' (west) or 148 (east); the head step is 40 up, so the ride ends at 19 or
2667               	; 	' 220. Those are the ART's numbers -- the foot tread is drawn at x 95-103
2668               	; 	' west and 152-160 east, the head tread at 23-31 and 224-232 -- so moving
2669               	; 	' the art without moving these puts the rider beside the staircase.
2670               	; 	'
2671               	; 	' THE PHASE MATTERS. The steps climb 1 px a frame and the animation runs
2672               	; 	' four 1 px phases, so the bottom step is 4 + escp px up, not 4. Boarding
2673               	; 	' without that term leaves the feet up to 3 px out of register with the
2674               	; 	' tread and the whole ride drifts, which is exactly what "he floats
2675               	; 	' beside the steps" looked like.
2676               	; 	CONST ESCFX = 91		' west foot: rider's x when boarding
2677      005B     const_ESCFX	equ >005b
2678               	; 	CONST ESCFXE = 148		' east foot
2679      0094     const_ESCFXE	equ >0094
2680               	; 	CONST ESCHX = 19		' west head: rider's x on arrival
2681      0013     const_ESCHX	equ >0013
2682               	; 	CONST ESCHXE = 220		' east head
2683      00DC     const_ESCHXE	equ >00dc
2684               	; 	CONST ESCRISE = 40		' floor to floor, and the ride's length
2685      0028     const_ESCRISE	equ >0028
2686               	;
2687               	; 	' TIMER UNITS PER KROOK, AND A UNIT IS NOT A SECOND. Measured off the
2688               	; 	' reference video (DESIGN.md 0m): the original counts 50 down to 0 and a
2689               	; 	' unit lasts 1.99 s, so a round is about 100 seconds. TICKFR below is
2690               	; 	' what makes it so here.
2691               	; 	CONST TIMEL = 50		' timer units per Krook
2692      0032     const_TIMEL	equ >0032
2693               	; 	' FRAMES PER TIMER UNIT. 120, not 60, and this is not cosmetic -- it is
2694               	; 	' what makes a round finishable. Everything that MOVES in this game is
2695               	; 	' paced per loop PASS, and the loop runs about 25 passes a second, so
2696               	; 	' Kelly's 4 px a pass is ~100 px/s (the reference's Kelly is 102, so the
2697               	; 	' speeds match). The timer, though, is paced by the frame DELTA -- real
2698               	; 	' wall-clock time. At 60 frames a unit the round was 50 real seconds
2699               	; 	' while Kelly's route to the roof takes about 72, so the clock ran out
2700               	; 	' before either of them could get there and every round ended on a
2701               	; 	' timeout. checkchase.py hid it by assuming 60 passes a second; it now
2702               	; 	' models the real rate.
2703               	; 	CONST TICKFR = 120
2704      0078     const_TICKFR	equ >0078
2705               	; 	' NINE TIMER UNITS -- not ten, and not nine seconds. Every source says a
2706               	; 	' cart, ball or radio costs "9 seconds", and what they mean is the number
2707               	; 	' on the HUD, because that is what the manual calls seconds. So the
2708               	; 	' DISPLAYED count drops by 9. A unit is about two real seconds
2709               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 0m), which makes one careless cart cost roughly eighteen --
2710               	; 	' close to a fifth of the round, and the reason the refractory latch
2711               	; 	' below matters so much.
2712               	; 	CONST HITPEN = 9		' timer units a cart / ball / radio costs
2713      0009     const_HITPEN	equ >0009
2714               	; 	' HOW LONG A HIT SOUNDS, IN LOOP PASSES -- and therefore how long the
2715               	; 	' store stands still for one. The two are the same number on purpose:
2716               	; 	' the freeze is meant to last exactly as long as the noise, so a change
2717               	; 	' to one that did not move the other would leave either a silent pause
2718               	; 	' or a sound playing over a resumed game. Passes, not frames, because
2719               	; 	' both counters are spent once per pass in sfx_tick and the main loop.
2720               	; 	CONST HITSND = 20
2721      0014     const_HITSND	equ >0014
2722               	; 	CONST HITREF = 45		' frames before the SAME obstacle can charge
2723      002D     const_HITREF	equ >002d
2724               	; 					' again. See coll_obst -- clearing the latch
2725               	; 					' on the first non-overlapping frame is not
2726               	; 					' enough, because a bouncing ball leaves
2727               	; 					' contact between bounces.
2728               	;
2729               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- tables
2730               	; 	DIM flry(4)			' floor surface y, by level
2731               	; 	DIM #bdst(4)			' band name-table offset, by level
2732               	; 	DIM #tsrc(15)			' template source offset, by template id
2733               	; 	' THE NES CANNOT READ ITS OWN VIDEO MEMORY BACK, so anything this
2734               	; 	' program does as read-modify-write needs the "read" to come from RAM
2735               	; 	' instead. WRTVRM on that target does not touch the PPU at all -- it
2736               	; 	' queues into PPUBUF for the NMI to flush -- so a read would be both
2737               	; 	' illegal during rendering and blind to everything still in the queue.
2738               	; 	'
2739               	; 	' The radar is the only read-modify-write on the PATTERN table: it ORs
2740               	; 	' pixel rows into its canvas characters, 208-255, eight bytes each.
2741               	; 	' 384 bytes of the NES's 1,227 free, and nothing on the other targets.
2742               	; 	#if NES
2743               	; 	DIM nsc(768)			' radar canvas pattern shadow, 48 tiles x 16
2744               	; 	DIM nesb(96)			' the escalator's six characters, staged for the NMI
2745               	; 	DIM nmsg(4)			' packed surrounding attribute halves for GAME OVER
2746               	; 	#endif
2747               	; 	DIM lv8(4)			' lv*8, so no multiply lands on an index
2748               	; 	DIM rhaz(16)			' packed hazard map, retained across deaths
2749               	; 	#if NES
2750               	; 	DIM jarc(30)			' 30 frames exactly: kjf wraps past 29, and NES RAM is full
2751               	; 	#else
2752               	; 	DIM jarc(32)			' the jump arc: 30 frames, apex 14
2753               	; 	#endif
2754               	; 	DIM msk(8)
2755               	;
2756               	; 	' EIGHT obstacle slots -- TWO per band, and that number is forced.
2757               	; 	'
2758               	; 	' The VDP shows four sprites per scanline and DROPS the rest by slot
2759               	; 	' order; it does not flicker them, they simply are not there. Three per
2760               	; 	' band was sized against Kelly alone (1 + 3 = 4) and forgot that HARRY
2761               	; 	' can be on that band too -- and when he is, the fifth sprite on his
2762               	; 	' scanline is the highest-numbered obstacle, which vanishes while still
2763               	; 	' being solid. An invisible thing that costs nine seconds is the worst
2764               	; 	' failure in the game and it only happens when the crook is next to you,
2765               	; 	' which is exactly when you are not looking at the floor.
2766               	; 	'
2767               	; 	' Kelly (slot 0) + Harry (slot 1) + two obstacles = four. Provably never
2768               	; 	' dropped, on any band, in any situation.
2769               	; 	'
2770               	; 	' ...AND THAT CAP IS ABOUT SPRITES, WHICH A RADIO IS NOT. The scanline
2771               	; 	' limit is the whole argument above, and it does not reach the radio: a
2772               	; 	' radio is four CHARACTERS stamped into the name table by draw_radios, it
2773               	; 	' costs no sprite, and the VDP will happily draw a hundred of them on one
2774               	; 	' line. The original puts up to THREE on a floor (assets/ref2600/hazards.md
2775               	; 	' measures them at three fixed positions), and the reason we had two was
2776               	; 	' this comment being read as a limit on hazards when it is a limit on
2777               	; 	' sprites.
2778               	; 	'
2779               	; 	' So there are TWELVE slots in two groups, and the split is deliberate:
2780               	; 	'
2781               	; 	'   0-7    two per band, band*2 + slot -- ANY kind, and these are the ones
2782               	; 	'          that own sprites 8-15 (propellers 16-23). Untouched.
2783               	; 	'   8-11   ONE per band, 8 + band -- RADIO OR EMPTY, never a sprite.
2784               	; 	'
2785               	; 	' Keeping the new slots in their own block rather than making the stride
2786               	; 	' three is what leaves draw_obst's `FOR di = 0 TO 7` and its `ds = di + 8`
2787               	; 	' exactly as they were. A stride of three would have scattered the
2788               	; 	' sprite-bearing slots to 0,1,3,4,6,7,9,10 and every sprite number in the
2789               	; 	' game would have had to be recomputed -- to place a thing that does not
2790               	; 	' use one.
2791               	; 	DIM obk(12)			' kind, 0 = empty
2792               	; 	DIM obx(12)			' x within the screen
2793               	; 	DIM obd(12)			' 0 = moving left, 1 = right
2794               	; 	DIM obh(12)			' art-bottom height above the slab
2795               	; 	DIM obc(12)			' cell column, radios only -- they are chars
2796               	; 	DIM obp(12)			' bounce phase, balls only
2797               	; 	DIM obht(12)			' hit refractory, per obstacle -- see coll_obst
2798               	;
2799               	; 	DIM cok(4)			' this screen's collectible, per band
2800               	; 	DIM coc(4)			' its column
2801               	; 	DIM takn(4)			' 32 bits: which bands have been cleaned out

2806               	; 	' Harry the same. NOTHING in this program is a world coordinate.

2811               	; 	' is needed to put text on a screen: draw the title immediately, then
2812               	; 	' define the store characters, the store colours, the escalator deck, the
2813               	; 	' radar canvas and eight sprite sets while the player reads it. None of
2814               	; 	' that is touched until new_game, so nothing was out of order.
2815               	; 	'
2816               	; 	' IT MADE THE TITLE APPEAR SOONER AND ARRIVE DEAD. A third of a second of
2817               	; 	' a finished screen that was not yet reading the keyboard -- long enough to
2818               	; 	' swallow the first digit of 8-3-8, and reported as a start press that did

2990               	;
2991               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- TITLE MUSIC
2992               	; 	' STREET from the tunes bench (sound/tunes), TI only. assets/genmusic.py
2993               	; 	' renders it into titlemusic.bas, which lives in BANK 2 beside the font.
2994               	; 	'
2995               	; 	' WHY BANK 2 IS SAFE FOR DATA READ UNDER THE ISR. The rule in CLAUDE.md 3A
2996               	; 	' is about the program switching banks while the ISR reads, and the main
2997               	; 	' loop DOES switch to bank 2 and back every pass (ti_cancel_key). The TI
2998               	; 	' music player handles that itself: PLAY records the page mapped at the
2999               	; 	' time (>7FFE), and every interrupt saves the current page, maps the
3000               	; 	' music's page to read the next row, and restores the saved one before
3001               	; 	' returning. So PLAY must run while bank 2 is SELECTED, and nothing else
3002               	; 	' needs to know. Read cvbasic_9900_prologue.asm (int_handler, music_play,
3003               	; 	' music_generate) before changing this.
3004               	; 	'
3005               	; 	' STOPPING IS TWO STATEMENTS AND BOTH MATTER. PLAY OFF silences the tune,
3006               	; 	' but the ISR keeps rewriting the chip every frame while a play MODE is
3007               	; 	' set (Structris' level_up note: its channels stuck) -- which would stomp
3008               	; 	' every sound effect in the game. PLAY NONE clears the mode, and the ISR
3009               	; 	' then leaves the chip alone. snd_off after it, so nothing the tune left
3010               	; 	' latched rings into the round.

3114               	; 	#if TI994A
3115               	; 	#else
3116               	; 	' MATCH THE TI'S LOOP RATE, AND DO IT HERE RATHER THAN ANYWHERE ELSE.
3117               	; 	'
3118               	; 	' Three things in this game are paced per LOOP PASS and must stay locked to
3119               	; 	' one another: the escalator's four-phase step animation, Kelly riding it
3120               	; 	' and Harry riding it. CLAUDE.md 3A is explicit that a cyclic animation can
3121               	; 	' only be stepped by ONE phase per pass -- step it by two and the direction
3122               	; 	' becomes unreadable, by three and the staircase visibly runs backwards --
3123               	; 	' so the riders have to be on the pass clock too, and changing any ONE of
3124               	; 	' the three decouples a rider from the tread he is standing on.
3125               	; 	'
3126               	; 	' The NES and Coleco builds run more passes per second than the TI, so the
3127               	; 	' escalator ran at that rate: correct, coupled, and far too fast. The only
3128               	; 	' change that keeps all three together is to the LOOP RATE itself. The TI
3129               	; 	' measures ~24 passes a second (CLAUDE.md 3A: 2,335 passes over ~98 s), so
3130               	; 	' a pass is 2.5 frames, and `nespw` alternates 2 and 3 to average it.
3131               	; 	'
3132               	; 	' IT IS A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING. A pass that already took longer than nespw
3133               	; 	' frames waits for nothing, so a heavy screen still runs at whatever rate
3134               	; 	' it can -- exactly as on the TI.
3135               	; nes_pace:
3136               	; 	#fd = FRAME - #lf
3137               	; 	IF #fd < nespw THEN
3138               	; 		WAIT
3139               	; 		GOTO nes_pace
3140               	; 	END IF
3141               	; 	nespw = 5 - nespw
3142               	; 	#endif
3143               	; 	#if TI994A
3144               	; 	BANK SELECT 2
3145 AFE2 04E0  34 	clr @>6008
     AFE4 6008     
3146               	; 	GOSUB ti_cancel_key
3147 AFE6 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     AFE8 AE2A

3202               	;
3203               	; 	' THE STORE STOPS FOR A HIT. THE CHASE DOES NOT.
3204               	; 	'
3205               	; 	' Nine seconds off the clock is the heaviest thing that happens in this
3206               	; 	' game and it used to happen in silence and in motion: the number
3207               	; 	' changed, a flash played, and the player kept running. Holding the
3208               	; 	' screen for exactly as long as the hit SOUNDS makes the penalty an event
3209               	; 	' rather than a bookkeeping entry -- the arcade's own idiom, and the
3210               	; 	' reason the 2600 original pauses here too.
3211               	; 	'
3212               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS RUNNING IS THE POINT. Harry is still escaping and the clock
3213               	; 	' is still burning, so the freeze is a cost and not a rest: stopping
3214               	; 	' those as well would turn the penalty into free time. It also keeps the
3215               	; 	' two things the player is racing on their own clocks, which is the whole
3216               	; 	' argument of section 0f-ter -- a pause that stopped the timer would make
3217               	; 	' the price of a hit depend on how long the pause happened to be.
3218               	; 	'
3219               	; 	' esc_tick stays with Harry, not with the store. He rides the escalator
3220               	; 	' on the animation's clock (CLAUDE.md: a rider and its cyclic animation
3221               	; 	' share one clock or the rider drifts off it), so freezing the steps
3222               	; 	' under a moving Harry would slide him up a stationary staircase.
3223               	; 	'
3224               	; 	' Kelly cannot be hit on an escalator or in the lift -- obstacles live on

3411               	; 	'
3412               	; 	' THIS IS THE TITLE'S COLOUR SHIFT ON A COLD BOOT. The store load above
3413               	; 	' gives BULB0..3 their colour bytes out of store_col, where the lamps are
3414               	; 	' white on DARK BLUE -- and dark blue maps to index 1, which on the title
3415               	; 	' page is P0's entry 1: GREEN. So the marquee came up as gold lamps on a
3416               	; 	' green ribbon.

3418               	; 	' It then fixed itself, one lamp at a time, because title_wait re-sends the
3419               	; 	' two lamps it changes with `#ncol = 0` and `nink = 3` -- ink 3 on index 0,
3420               	; 	' the backdrop. After two full rotations all four had been rewritten and
3421               	; 	' the green was gone. Measured on a cold boot: green pixels peak eight
3422               	; 	' frames in and reach zero eleven frames later, which is exactly "something
3423               	; 	' is initialised later".

3425               	; 	' Sending them here in the form the marquee uses means the first frame of

3851               	; 	' ======================================================================
3852               	; 	' TITLE
3853               	; 	' ======================================================================
3854               	; 	' DRAWING THE TITLE AND WAITING ON IT ARE TWO ROUTINES, because the boot
3855               	; 	' does something between them: the rest of setup runs while this is on
3856               	; 	' screen. They used to be one, which is why the title could not be shown
3857               	; 	' until everything was ready.
3858               	; 	' THE TITLE IS A DISPLAY LIST IN A ROM BANK, not twelve PRINT ATs.
3859               	; 	'
3860               	; 	' CVBasic embeds a string literal in the FIXED AREA, which is the only
3861               	; 	' budget that cannot be grown -- linkticart writes exactly three loader
3862               	; 	' pages and discards the rest, and they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
3863               	; 	' >A000 rather than cart ROM. 190 characters of title text were sitting
3864               	; 	' in the scarcest place in the program.
3865               	; 	'
3866               	; 	' AND THE REAL POINT IS WHAT IT COSTS NEXT TIME. With the text in a
3867               	; 	' table, changing what the title says or where it sits is an edit to
3868               	; 	' assets/gentitle.py and a rebuild. It costs bank bytes, of which there
3869               	; 	' are thousands, instead of fixed-area bytes, of which there are tens.
3870               	; 	'
3871               	; 	' The table is `row, col, length, bytes...` with 255 to end. ROW AND
3872               	; 	' COLUMN rather than a 16-bit screen offset, because reassembling one
3873               	; 	' from two bytes needs a multiply, and on the TMS9900 MPY clobbers r0 --
3874               	; 	' the next line that reads the product's variable gets the HIGH word
3875               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). Five doublings have no such hazard and are smaller.
3876               	; 	#if NES
3877               	; title_background:
3878               	; 	' CLS resets attributes to green P0. Both title and setup need blue P2.
3879               	; 	#nav = 9152			' $23C0

3881               	; 		VPOKE #nav,170

3884               	; 	RETURN
3885               	; 	#endif

3888               	; 	' end-of-round message boxes are the same shape -- runs of characters at
3889               	; 	' fixed positions -- so they are the same data format and the same dozen
3890               	; 	' statements. A caller sets the address and calls; nothing here knows
3891               	; 	' which screen it is drawing.

4185               	; 	'
4186               	; 	' His escape route ZIGZAGS -- east along floor 2 to its escalator, WEST
4187               	; 	' along floor 3 to that one, then east again along the roof to the door.
4188               	; 	' From the lift on screen 3 that is 5,120 px against the 4,208 he walked
4189               	; 	' from screen 7, so at his old 1.75 px a pass he needed 105 s of a 100 s
4190               	; 	' round: he could never escape at all, and one of the two loss conditions
4191               	; 	' would quietly have stopped existing. This block used to say exactly that
4192               	; 	' and conclude the lift was impossible. It was impossible AT THAT SPEED.
4193               	; 	'

4195               	; 	' per pass is worth about TEN SECONDS of his route, so the two candidate
4196               	; 	' values straddled the buzzer with nothing in between:
4197               	; 	'
4198               	; 	'   2.00 px/pass   escapes at 102.4 s of a 100 s round   never escapes
4199               	; 	'   2.25 px/pass   escapes at  91.0 s                    nine seconds early
4200               	; 	'

4203               	; 	' silently delivered 2.00 and he fell two thirds of a screen short of his
4204               	; 	' own escape. See the accumulator comment for the full account.

4477               	;
4478               	; 	' ======================================================================
4479               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
4480               	; 	' ======================================================================
4481               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
4482               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
4483               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
4484               	; 	' of running.
4485               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
4486               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
4487               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
4488               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
4489               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
4490               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
4491               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
4492               	; 	'
4493               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
4494               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
4495               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
4496               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
4497               	; 	'
4498               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
4499               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
4500               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
4501               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
4502               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
4503               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
4504               	; 	'
4505               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
4506               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
4507               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
4508               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
4509               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
4510               	; 	'
4511               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
4512               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
4513               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).

4661               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS

4663               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is

4673               	; 	'

5312               	; 			' per screen where the divide would run per obstacle -- so
5313               	; 			' the loop is the cheaper of the two, and the only one that
5314               	; 			' cannot be got wrong by a rounding rule.
5315               	; 			obc(li) = 0
5316 BBD8 04C1  14 	clr r1

     BBDC 220A

     BBE2 229C     
5320 BBE4 D401  30 	movb r1,*r0
5321               	; 			' PER KIND, not one global speed (see start_krook).
5322               	; 			' THE SPEED IS A PROPERTY OF THE KIND, and obs() only ever
5323               	; 			' held a copy of it -- set from the kind here, zeroed for a
5324               	; 			' radio below, and read in one place. upd_obst derives it
5325               	; 			' from obk() instead, which is 8 bytes of RAM back and one
5326               	; 			' fewer thing that can disagree with itself.
5327               	; 			' THEY COME FROM THE FAR SIDE. Kelly walked into this screen
5328               	; 			' from one edge, so the obstacles start at the OTHER edge and
5329               	; 			' run toward him. Crossing a seam then always presents an
5330               	; 			' ONCOMING stream, never a set of backs he has to catch up
5331               	; 			' with -- and it means the direction he is travelling is
5332               	; 			' always the direction the danger comes from.
5333               	; 			'
5334               	; 			' The table's x becomes a stagger from that edge rather than
5335               	; 			' an absolute position, and the slot index spreads them out
5336               	; 			' so they arrive in sequence instead of as one wall.
5337               	; 			'
5338               	; 			' THE SECOND ONE IS A FIXED DISTANCE BEHIND THE FIRST, AND
5339               	; 			' THAT DISTANCE IS SET BY THE JUMP.
5340               	; 			'
5341               	; 			' It used to be `(lx AND 63) + 64` -- a masked byte out of
5342               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between
5343               	; 			' the two hazards was whatever those two bytes happened to
5344               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it
5345               	; 			' came out 46, 46, 70, 70, 70 px. Screens 2 and 4 flank the
5346               	; 			' elevator, so the store had a visibly tighter pair on one
5347               	; 			' side of it than the other, which is exactly how it was
5348               	; 			' reported from play.
5349               	; 			'
5350               	; 			' Both numbers are too small, which is the real fault. Kelly
5351               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64
5352               	; 			' px a FRAME, and the jump is airborne 28 frames, so a jump
5353               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At
5354               	; 			' 46 or 70 there is NO screen where he can land between the
5355               	; 			' two: he clears the first and comes down on the second.
5356               	; 			'
5357               	; 			' HAZGAP is that distance with margin, and it agrees with
5358               	; 			' the original to within 4 px (see the CONST). The pairing
5359               	; 			' is now a fact about the jump rather than an accident of
5360               	; 			' two bytes. assets/checkspace.py measures it and fails the
5361               	; 			' build.
5362               	; 			' THE SECOND SLOT IS MEASURED FROM THE FIRST, not from its
5363               	; 			' own table byte. Adding HAZGAP to its own `lx AND 63` would
5364               	; 			' still leave the GAP varying by up to 63 px between screens
5365               	; 			' -- the same fault in a politer form, and the reason the two
5366               	; 			' sides of the elevator differed in the first place. Holding
5367               	; 			' slot 0's stagger and adding to that makes the gap exactly
5368               	; 			' HAZGAP on every screen, while slot 0 still lands wherever
5369               	; 			' the table puts it, so the placement variety is untouched.
5370               	; 			' DERIVED FROM THE BAND, not stored. The table used to carry

5471               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
5472               	; 			'
5473               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
5474               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
5475               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
5476               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
5477               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
5478               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
5479               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
5480               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
5481               	; 			'
5482               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
5483               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
5484               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
5485               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
5486               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
5487               	; 			'
5488               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
5489               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
5490               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
5491               	; 			'
5492               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
5493               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
5494               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
5495               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
5496               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
5497               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
5498               	; 			' obp is a BALL-only field: upd_obst reads it under an
5499               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every
5500               	; 			' ball has it computed below. It was seeded here from a
5501               	; 			' table byte that no longer exists, and for anything but
5502               	; 			' a ball that seed was never read.

7925               	;
7926               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
7927               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
7928               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
7929               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
7930               	; 	'
7931               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
7932               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
7933               	; 	'
7934               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
7935               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
7936               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
7937               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
7938               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
7939               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
7940               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
7941               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
7942               	; 	' merged object.
7943               	; 	'
7944               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
7945               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
7946               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
7947               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
7948               	; 	'
7949               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
7950               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
7951               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
7952               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
7953               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
7954               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
7955               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
7956               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
7957               	; 	'
7958               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
7959               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
7960               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
7961               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
7962               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
7963               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
7964               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
7965               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
7966               	; 	' its bottom half together.
7967               	; 	'
7968               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
7969               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
7970               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
7971               	; 	#if NES
7972               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
7973               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
7974               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
7975               	; 	'
7976               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
7977               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
7978               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
7979               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
7980               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
7981               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
7982               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
7983               	; 	'
7984               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
7985               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
7986               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
7987               	; 	'
7988               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
7989               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
7990               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
7991               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
7992               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
7993               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
7994               	; 	'                   the whole time.
7995               	; 	'
7996               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
7997               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
7998               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
7999               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8000               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8001               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8002               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8003               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8004               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8005               	; 	'
8006               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8007               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8008               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8009               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8010               	; 	'
8011               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8012               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8013               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8014               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8015               	; nes_swp16:
8016               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8017               	; 	'
8018               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8019               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8020               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8021               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8022               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8023               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8024               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8025               	; 	'
8026               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8027               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8028               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8029               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8030               	; 	'
8031               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8032               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8033               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8034               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is

8068               	; nes_def:
8069               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8070               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8071               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8072               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8073               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8074               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8075               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8076               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8077               	; 	RETURN
8078               	;
8079               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8080               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8081               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
8082               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
8083               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor

8092               	; 	'

8860               	; 	' ONE ACCUMULATOR PER KIND, NOT PER SLOT. Every hazard of a kind moves at
8861               	; 	' that kind's speed, so three calls a pass serve all eight slots.

8903               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.
8904               	; 	'
8905               	; 	' The jump has always advanced by the frame delta (`kjf = kjf + fdv`) while
8906               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
8907               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
8908               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
8909               	; 	'
8910               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
8911               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
8912               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
8913               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
8914               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to

9180               	;
9181               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
9182               	; 	'
9183               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
9184               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
9185               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
9186               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
9187               	; 	'
9188               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
9189               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
9190               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
9191               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
9192               	; 	'
9193               	; 	' Three drains support up to 192/64 units per frame. The remainder
9194               	; 	' is below 64, so the byte addition cannot exceed 255. Planes use
9195               	; 	' two-pixel units and double the result outside this shared routine.
9196               	; 	' Other actors retain pixel units and their existing movement rates.
9197               	; 	'
9198               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
9199               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
9200               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
9201               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
9202               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
9203               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.
9204               	; pace_step:
9205               cvb_PACE_STEP

9708               	;
9709               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
9710               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
9711               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
9712               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
9713               	; 	' runs every pass.
9714               	; 	'
9715               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
9716               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
9717               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
9718               	; 	'
9719               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
9720               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
9721               	; 	'
9722               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
9723               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
9724               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
9725               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
9726               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
9727               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
9728               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
9729               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
9730               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
9731               	; 	'
9732               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
9733               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
9734               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
9735               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
9736               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
9737               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
9738               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
9739               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,

9839               	;
9840               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
9841               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
9842               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
9843               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
9844               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
9845               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
9846               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
9847               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
9848               	; 	'
9849               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
9850               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
9851               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
9852               	; 	'
9853               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
9854               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
9855               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
9856               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
9857               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
9858               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
9859               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
9860               	; 	'
9861               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
9862               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
9863               	; 	'
9864               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
9865               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
9866               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
9867               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
9868               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
9869               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
9870               	; 	'
9871               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
9872               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
9873               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
9874               	; 	' before any of this.
9875               	; 	'
9876               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
9877               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
9878               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the

10345               	;
10346               	; 	' ======================================================================
10347               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
10348               	; 	' ======================================================================
10349               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
10350               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
10351               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
10352               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
10353               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
10354               	; 	'
10355               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
10356               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
10357               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
10358               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
10359               	; 	' broken.
10360               	; 	'
10361               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
10362               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
10363               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
10364               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
10365               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
10366               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
10367               	; 	'
10368               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
10369               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
10370               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
10371               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
10372               	; coll_obst:
10373               cvb_COLL_OBST
10374               	; 	IF klst = ST_ESC THEN RETURN		' riding is invincible, per the

     DD38 21B8     
10847               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
10848               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
10849               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
10850               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
10851               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
10852               	; 	' away from.
10853               	; 	'
10854               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
10855               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
10856               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
10857               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
10858               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
10859               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
10860               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
10861               	; 	'
10862               	; 	' NOTHING RESTORES IT HERE. load_band repopulates the band from the
10863               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so
10864               	; 	' "until the screen is re-entered" costs no state and no timer: leave and
10865               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.
10866               	; 	'
10867               	; 	' THE CALL ITSELF IS IN THE MAIN LOOP, at the end of the freeze -- see
10868               	; 	' the hfz block there for why.
10869               	; 	' A HIT DOES NOT END A JUMP. This used to force ST_RUN and zero the arc,
10870               	; 	' which dropped him straight down out of mid-air onto whatever he happened
10871               	; 	' to be over -- and since the arc is ballistic and ignores the stick once
10872               	; 	' he is airborne (0l), that read as the game taking the controls away
10873               	; 	' rather than as a hit landing. The penalty is the nine units and the
10874               	; 	' hit sound; where he comes down is still his own arc.
10875               	; 	'
10876               	; 	' A ducking Kop is still stood up, because the crouch is a held pose and
10877               	; 	' there is nothing to interrupt.
10878               	; 	IF klst <> ST_JUMP THEN

12236               	; 	' THE SCANNER
12237               	; 	' ======================================================================
12238               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
12239               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table

12241               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
12242               	; 	'

12244               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
12245               	; 	'

12248               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
12249               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
12250               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
12251               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
12252               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
12253               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
12254               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
12255               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so

12282               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
12283               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
12284               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
12285               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
12286               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
12287               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
12288               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
12289               	; 	'
