12291               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
12292               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
12293               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
12294               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
12295               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
12296               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

12310               	; 	#if NES
12311               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
12312               	; 	'
12313               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
12314               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
12315               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
12316               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
12317               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
12318               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
12319               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
12320               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
12321               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
12322               	; 	'
12323               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
12324               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
12325               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
12326               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
12327               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
12328               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
12329               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
12330               	; 	'
12331               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
12332               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
12333               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
12334               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
12335               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
12336               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
12337               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
12338               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
12339               	; 	' with room to spare.
12340               	; 	'
12341               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
12342               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
12343               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
12344               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
12345               	; 	WAIT
12346               	; 	#endif

12348               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them

12350               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
12351               	; 	' 7 an east one.
12352               	; 	'

12354               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
12355               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
12356               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
12357               	; 	'
12358               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
12359               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
12360               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the

12693               	;
12694               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
12695               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
12696               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
12697               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
12698               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
12699               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
12700               	; 	'
12701               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
12702               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
12703               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
12704               	; 	'
12705               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
12706               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
12707               	; 	'   +2  GREY
12708               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
12709               	; 	'
12710               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
12711               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
12712               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
12713               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
12714               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
12715               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
12716               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
12717               	; 	'
12718               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
12719               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
12720               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.
12721               	; 	'
12722               	; 	' The dots are erased by ANDing their bits out, so anything sharing a row
12723               	; 	' with one is rubbed away wherever an actor has passed -- which is why
12724               	; 	' scan_escs and scan_elev redraw every tick rather than once.

12994               	; 	'

12996               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
12997               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
12998               	; 	'

13000               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
13001               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
13002               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,

13004               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.

13042               	; 	' THE ONE READ-MODIFY-WRITE ON THE PATTERN TABLE. The radar ORs a
13043               	; 	' pixel row into a canvas character, so it has to know what is already
13044               	; 	' there. On the NES that read comes from nsc, which scan_wipe zeroed

13050               	; 	' all in scan_escs). On the TI they are drawn as INK and coloured black by

13052               	; 	' 0 set everywhere, see scan_wipe. Black is index 2: clear plane 0 and
13053               	; 	' set plane 1 for the same pixels. Preserve the caller's pattern address.
13054               	; 	'

13167               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13168               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a

13170               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13171               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13172               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).

13175               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13176               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13177               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13178               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13179               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13180               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13181               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13182               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13183               	; 	'
13184               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13185               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13186               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13187               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13188               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13189               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13190               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on

13192               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13193               	; 	'
13194               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13195               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13196               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13197               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13198               	; 	'

13836               	;
13837               	; #if NES
13838               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
13839               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
13840               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
13841               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
13842               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
13843               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
13844               	; 	'
13845               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
13846               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
13847               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
13848               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
13849               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
13850               	; 	'
13851               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
13852               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
13853               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
13854               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
13855               	; 	'
13856               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
13857               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
13858               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
13859               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
13860               	; 	' these beside it.
13861               	; 	'
13862               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
13863               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
13864               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
13865               	; nes_boxatt:
13866               	; 	WAIT
13867               	; 	IF #nav = 9178 THEN
13868               	; 		' GAME OVER begins in the lower half of one attribute row.
13869               	; 		' Preserve the surrounding halves from the actual screen upload.
13870               	; 		FOR nai = 0 TO 3
13871               	; 			nink = (nmsg(nai) AND 15) OR 80
13872               	; 			VPOKE #nav,nink
13873               	; 			#nsrc = #nav + 8
13874               	; 			nink = (nmsg(nai) AND 240) OR 15
13875               	; 			VPOKE #nsrc,nink
13876               	; 			#nav = #nav + 1
13877               	; 		NEXT nai
13878               	; 		#nsrc = 8712		' PPU row 16 col 8, bottom border
13879               	; 	ELSE
13880               	; 		' Skyline P1/P2 split: retain every colour outside the box.
13881               	; 		FOR nai = 0 TO 3
13882               	; 			VPOKE #nav,165
13883               	; 			#nav = #nav + 1
13884               	; 		NEXT nai
13885               	; 		#nsrc = 8392		' PPU row 6 col 8, bottom border
13886               	; 	END IF
13887               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 15
13888               	; 		VPOKE #nsrc,CH_ECAR
13889               	; 		#nsrc = #nsrc + 1
13890               	; 	NEXT nai
13891               	; 	WAIT
13892               	; 	RETURN
13893               	;
13894               	; nes_attr:
13895               	; 	' nesb holds attributes only during draw_screen; flush before reuse by
13896               	; 	' escalator or marquee CHR uploads. One 64-byte copy fits one vblank.

14377               	;
14378               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
14379               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
14380               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
14381               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
14382               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
14383               	; 	'
14384               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
14385               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
14386               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
14387               	; 	'
14388               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
14389               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
14390               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
14391               	; 	'
14392               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
14393               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
14394               	; 	'
14395               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
14396               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
14397               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
14398               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
14399               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
14400               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
14401               	; 	'
14402               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
14403               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
14404               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
14405               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
14406               	; 	'
14407               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
14408               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
14409               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
14410               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)

14554               	;
14555               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
14556               	; 	'
14557               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
14558               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
14559               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
14560               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
14561               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
14562               	; 	'
14563               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
14564               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
14565               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
14566               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
14567               	; 	' counting stops.
14568               	;
14569               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
14570               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
14571               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
14572               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
14573               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
14574               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
14575               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
14576               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
14577               	; 	'
14578               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
14579               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
14580               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14581               	;

14624 F256 F06C     	data cvb_TIME_SHOW
14625               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
14626               	; 	'
14627               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
14628               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
14629               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
14630               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
14631               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
14632               	; 	'
14633               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
14634               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
14635               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
14636               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
14637               	; 	'
14638               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
14639               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
14640               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
14641               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
14642               	; 	'
14643               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
14644               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
14645               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
14646               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
14647               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
14648               	; 	'
14649               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
14650               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
14651               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
14652               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
14653               	; 	'
14654               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout
14655               	; 	' serve both cases. Losing a life draws three rows around it; losing the
14656               	; 	' last one draws two more ON TOP, so GAME OVER appears above the reason
14657               	; 	' rather than replacing it. Printing the reason at a different row for each
14658               	; 	' case would need `PRINT AT` with a variable, and every other PRINT in this
14659               	; 	' program uses a constant.
14660               	; 	#if NES
14661               	; 	' FLUSH THE PASS BEFORE DRAWING A BOX. PPUBUF accumulates for a whole loop
14662               	; 	' pass and is emptied by one NMI, so a message box -- sixty-four cells,
14663               	; 	' sixty-four single-byte descriptors -- was landing in the same vblank as

14932               	;
14933               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
14934               	; 	'
14935               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
14936               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
14937               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
14938               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
14939               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
14940               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
14941               	; 	'
14942               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
14943               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
14944               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
14945               	; 	'
14946               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
14947               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
14948               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
14949               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
14950               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
14951               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
14952               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
14953               	; 	'
14954               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
14955               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
14956               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
14957               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
14958               	; 	'
14959               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
14960               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
14961               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
14962               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
14963               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
14964               	; 	'
14965               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
14966               	; 	' did not finish.
14967               	; pause_beat:

15020               	; 	' `SOUND ch,f,0` the last tone sustains for ever. And the second argument
15021               	; 	' is a 10-BIT DIVISOR, max 1023: SMALLER IS HIGHER, so a rising sweep is
15022               	; 	' written as a falling number and anything over 1023 is silently masked
15023               	; 	' to an unrelated pitch.

15028               	; 	' fewer statements -- and the fixed area was 14 bytes OVER when they were
15029               	; 	' written separately. Nothing else sets sfj, and if a jump and a plane
15030               	; 	' landed in one pass the last writer would win, which is academic: the
15031               	; 	' plane ends the round.

15407               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
15408               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
15409               	;
15410               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
15411               	; 	'
15412               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
15413               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
15414               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
15415               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
15416               	; 	'
15417               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
15418               	; 	'
15419               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
15420               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
15421               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
15422               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
15423               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
15424               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
15425               	; 	'
15426               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
15427               	; 	'
15428               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
15429               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
15430               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
15431               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
15432               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
15433               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
15434               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
15435               	; 	'
15436               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
15437               	; 	'
15438               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
15439               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
15440               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
15441               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
15442               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
15443               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
15444               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
15445               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
15446               	; 	'
15447               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
15448               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
15449               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
15450               	; 	'
15451               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
15452               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
15453               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
15454               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
15455               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
15456               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
15457               	; 	'
15458               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
15459               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
15460               	; 	'
15461               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
15462               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
15463               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
15464               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
15465               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
15466               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
15467               	; 	'
15468               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
15469               	; 	'
15470               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
15471               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
15472               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
15473               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
15474               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
15475               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not
15476               	; 	' back to 7.

     F898 F874     
15801               	;
15802               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
15803               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
15804               	; 	'
15805               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
15806               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
15807               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
15808               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
15809               	; 	'
15810               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
15811               	; 	'
15812               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
15813               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
15814               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
15815               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
15816               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
15817               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
15818               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
15819               	; 	'
15820               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
15821               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
15822               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
15823               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
15824               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
15825               	; 	'
15826               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
15827               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
15828               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
15829               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
15830               	; 	#if TI994A
15831               	; 	BANK 2
15832      0764     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

16788               	;
16789               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- GAME MUSIC
16790               	; 	' CHASE (game_tune, genmusic.py) plays during a round on PLAY SIMPLE NO
16791               	; 	' DRUMS: TWO voices on channels 0 and 1 only. The TI effects split by
16792               	; 	' channel -- 0 the jump warble (swt), 1 hits and the escape (sht), 2
16793               	; 	' prizes/lives/tally, noise the footsteps -- so only jumps and hits
16794               	; 	' collide, and those DUCK the music: PLAY NONE freezes the player where
16795               	; 	' it is (it only clears music_mode; the song position is untouched), and
16796               	; 	' PLAY SIMPLE NO DRUMS resumes from the same note once they end.
16797               	; 	'
16798               	; 	' The test runs BEFORE sfx_tick writes anything, and counts the pending
16799               	; 	' latches (sfj/sfh/sfe) as well as the running counters, so the player
16800               	; 	' has let go of the channel before the effect's first write -- otherwise
16801               	; 	' the next vblank would stomp that first frame.
16802               	; 	'
16803               	; 	' Called from the main loop only, never from pause_beat: the round-end
16804               	; 	' pause is effects-only (pause_beat stops the music on entry).
16805               	; 	'
16806               	; 	' IT LIVES IN BANK 2 and the main loop maps bank 2 around the call: the
16807               	; 	' fixed area's UNOPTIMISED first pass had 156 bytes left and this body
16808               	; 	' did not fit. A bonus: PLAY game_tune runs with bank 2 already mapped,
16809               	; 	' which is the page the player records for the tune. Nothing here may
16810               	; 	' BANK SELECT (it would unmap itself).
16811               	; music_duck:
16812               cvb_MUSIC_DUCK
16813               	; 	IF musen = 0 THEN RETURN	' M on the title turned music off

16821               	; 	#if NES
16822               	; 	' NES RAM IS FULL TO THE BYTE, so the NES keeps no gms/gmp/gmb: its whole
16823               	; 	' music state is nai -- 0 playing, 1 ducked, 2 not started. nai is NES
16824               	; 	' scratch that is idle here: the title's A toggle uses it (and treats 2
16825               	; 	' like a held A), and the round-end message boxes use it only after the
16826               	; 	' round's music is over and before music_stop sets it back to 2.
16827               	; 	IF nai = 2 THEN nai = 0 : PLAY SIMPLE NO DRUMS : PLAY game_tune
16828               	; 	' Same test as below, branching instead of setting gmb, plus the channel
16829               	; 	' owners the NES adds (the bugle on 0, the prize on 1 -- nes_apu.asm).
16830               	; 	' ONE TEST, NOT NINE. Every one of these is an unsigned byte, so "any is
16831               	; 	' non-zero" is their bitwise OR: one load and eight ORAs, about 35
16832               	; 	' bytes, where nine `IF x > 0 THEN GOTO` cost about 105 on the 6502 --
16833               	; 	' part of what let the NES title play the whole of STREET. (A bitwise OR
16834               	; 	' of VALUES, not of comparisons, so the TI's AND/OR hazard does not
16835               	; 	' apply; and this block is NES-only anyway.)
16836               	; 	IF swt OR sht OR sfj OR sfh OR sfe OR spt OR spz OR sfk OR sfp THEN GOTO md_busy
16837               	; 	IF nai = 0 THEN RETURN
16838               	; 	nai = 0
16839               	; 	PLAY SIMPLE NO DRUMS

17138               	;
17139               	;
17140               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
17141               	; 	'
17142               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
17143               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
17144               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
17145               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
17146               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
17147               	; 	'
17148               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
17149               	; 	'
17150               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
17151               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
17152               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
17153               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
17154               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
17155               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
17156               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
17157               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
17158               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
17159               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
17160               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
17161               	; 	'
17162               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
17163               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory
17164               	; 	' about keyboard noise that led to a filter which ate real presses.
17165               	; 	'
17166               	; 	' If a stuck axis ever does appear it will be obvious -- the player will
17167               	; 	' duck or ride the lift without asking -- and the guard is in the history.
17168               	;
17169               	; title_input:

17172               	; 	' this is the moment the game starts listening -- and it is a whole
17173               	; 	' second after the title appears.
17174               	; 	'
17175               	; 	' title_draw runs early on purpose (DESIGN.md 0d-nonies) so the screen
17176               	; 	' arrives instead of filling in, but setup_rest, init_tables and the
17177               	; 	' ALPHA LOCK sample all run AFTER it. For about a second the title is up,
17178               	; 	' finished, and completely deaf. A player types 8-3-8 into that window and
17179               	; 	' the first digit lands in nothing -- then a following 3-8 completes the
17180               	; 	' code, because the 8 they typed second is still standing as state. That

17291 69D8 A684     	data wait
17292               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
17293               	; 	'
17294               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
17295               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
17296               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
17297               	; 	' picture.
17298               	; 	'
17299               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
17300               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
17301               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
17302               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
17303               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
17304               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
17305               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
17306               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
17307               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
17308               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
17309               	; 	' same picture.
17310               	; 	'
17311               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
17312               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
17313               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
17314               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
17315               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.
17316               	; 	bfr = bfr - 1
17317 69DA D020  34 	movb @cvb_BFR,r0
     69DC 2086

17337               	; 		' therefore never services, so the game's own WAIT then waits for

17383               	; 		#if NES
17384               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
17385               	; 		'
17386               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
17387               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
17388               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
17389               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
17390               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
17391               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.
17392               	; 		'
17393               	; 		' So every step darkened two lamps and lit none, and the sign walked
17394               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
17395               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
17396               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
17397               	; 		'
17398               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
17399               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
17400               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
17401               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
17402               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.
17403               	; 		#nesb = #nesb + 16
17404               	; 		#nsrc = VARPTR bulb_off(0)
17405               	; 		nchr = bcode
17406               	; 		ncnt = 1
17407               	; 		ntab = 1
17408               	; 		#ncol = 0
17409               	; 		nink = 3
17410               	; 		GOSUB nes_escd			' queued -- see the note above
17411               	; 		#nesb = #nesb - 16
17412               	; 		#endif
17413               	; 		#if COLECOVISION
17414               	; 		DEFINE CHAR bcode,1,bulb_off
17415               	; 		#endif

17641               	;
17642               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
17643               	; 	'
17644               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
17645               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
17646               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
17647               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
17648               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
17649               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
17650               	; 	'
17651               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
17652               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
17653               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
17654               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
17655               	; 	'
17656               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
17657               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
17658               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page
17659               	; 	' ======================================================================
17660               	; 	' A NEW GAME / A NEW KROOK
17661               	; 	' ======================================================================
17662               	;
17663               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- MOVED TO BANK 2
17664               	; 	' setup_font and init_tables run ONCE, at power-on, and read nothing from
17665               	; 	' bank 1 -- so on the TI they live here, in bank 2, and the caller selects
17666               	; 	' bank 2 around the GOSUB. They moved to make room for the TI music player
17667               	; 	' (title music, ~1.2 KB of runtime in the fixed area): with it, the
17668               	; 	' UNOPTIMISED first assembly ran past >FFFF and xas99 rejected branches
17669               	; 	' before shortbranches.py could run (CLAUDE.md 3A, TI short-branch note).
17670               	; 	' A routine placed here must not BANK SELECT (it would unmap itself) and
17671               	; 	' must not read bank 1: init_tables' one bank-1 read, jarc_tbl, stayed
17672               	; 	' behind as init_jarc. On ColecoVision and NES this is ordinary code.
17673               	; setup_font:
17674               cvb_SETUP_FONT
17675               	; 	' Flicker stays OFF. CVBasic's is all-or-nothing -- it rotates all 32
17676               	; 	' slots, so Kelly would strobe too, and he is the one thing the player
17677               	; 	' must never lose. He is sprite 0 instead: the VDP drops the
17678               	; 	' HIGHEST-numbered sprites on an over-full scanline, so slot 0 is the
17679               	; 	' one slot that can never disappear.

17704               	;
17705               	; 	#if NES
17706               	; 	' THE NES'S TWO STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCES, SETTLED ONCE, HERE.
17707               	; 	'
17708               	; 	' 1. WHERE THE PATTERNS LIVE. In 8x16 sprite mode the sprite pattern table
17709               	; 	'    is chosen by bit 0 of each OAM tile byte and the PPUCTRL bit is
17710               	; 	'    ignored -- and every pattern number in this game is a multiple of
17711               	; 	'    four, so that bit is always 0 and the sprites are nailed to $0000.
17712               	; 	'    nes_bgbank therefore moves the BACKGROUND to $1000 rather than trying
17713               	; 	'    to move the sprites, which also lands the background patterns at
17714               	; 	'    address 4096, exactly where the TMS bitmap mode's third screen third
17715               	; 	'    had them -- so the radar's pattern writes need a stride and nothing
17716               	; 	'    else.
17717               	; 	'
17718               	; 	' 2. COLOUR DOES NOT MAP AND IS NOT PRETENDED TO. The NES colours in 16x16
17719               	; 	'    attribute blocks; this game colours per character, two colours a
17720               	; 	'    cell. So the store is drawn in ONE ink and the actors get four
17721               	; 	'    palettes, picked by the low two bits of the colour argument the
17722               	; 	'    SPRITE statements already pass -- 1 (black) -> dark grey, 4/8 (blue)
17723               	; 	'    -> blue, 14 (grey) -> grey, 11/15 (skin, white) -> white. Nothing in
17724               	; 	'    the game source has to know.
17725               	; 	ASM JSR nes_bgbank
17726               	; 	ASM JSR nes_apuon
17727               	;
17728               	; 	' Grey is shared index 0 during gameplay. Other indices are per region.
17729               	; 	' gennescolor.py assigns P3 only to counter quadrants, retaining green
17730               	; 	' wall and gold floor colours. Fixtures with black outlines use P0.
17731               	; 	PALETTE 1,26			' P0: green, black, gold
17732               	; 	PALETTE 2,15			' black escalators and fixture outlines
17733               	; 	PALETTE 3,40
17734               	; 	PALETTE 5,1			' P1 HUD/upper skyline: blue, pink, gold
17735               	; 	PALETTE 6,36
17736               	; 	PALETTE 7,40
17737               	; 	PALETTE 9,38			' P2 lower skyline: orange, black, gold
17738               	; 	PALETTE 10,1			' unused skyline index 2: navy message bottom border
17739               	; 	PALETTE 11,40
17740               	; 	PALETTE 13,26			' P3 counters: green, blue, gold
17741               	; 	PALETTE 14,1			' same navy in counter quadrants
17742               	; 	PALETTE 15,40
17743               	;
17744               	; 	' AND FOUR FOR THE ACTORS, which DO get one each because a sprite carries
17745               	; 	' its own palette number. nes_spal maps the TMS colour every SPRITE
17746               	; 	' statement already passes onto these four.
17747               	; 	PALETTE 17,18			' 0 -- blue   Kelly's trousers
17748               	; 	PALETTE 21,15			' 1 -- black  hats, Harry's stripes, the Kop's dot.
17749               	; 					' FIFTEEN, NOT ZERO: on this palette $0F is
17750               	; 					' black and $00 is a dark GREY, so every hat
17751               	; 					' and every stripe was coming out grey.
17752               	; 	PALETTE 22,23			' black sprite palette, index 2: brown suitcase outline
17753               	; 	PALETTE 25,39			' 2 -- skin   faces and the biplane
17754               	; 	PALETTE 26,16			' 2 colour 2 -- GREY, the lift car on the radar
17755               	; 	' AND THE BALL IS RED, which it already is on the TI: C_BALL is TMS 8,
17756               	; 	' medium red. nes_spal sends that to sprite palette 2, and palette 2's
17757               	; 	' colour ONE is the skin tone -- so on this machine the ball came out the
17758               	; 	' same pale orange as a face.
17759               	; 	'
17760               	; 	' A sprite here is ONE bitplane, so its pixels are whichever index the
17761               	; 	' upload writes and the OAM byte only chooses the palette. The lift car on
17762               	; 	' the radar already solved this: it is uploaded with `nink = 2` and reads
17763               	; 	' palette 2's second entry. The ball does the same with the THIRD, which
17764               	; 	' nothing else uses.
17765               	; 	PALETTE 27,22			' 2 colour 3 -- RED, the bouncing balls
17766               	; 	PALETTE 29,48			' 3 -- white  Harry, the carts, the lift car
17767               	;
17768               	; 	#endif
17769               	; 	#if TI994A
17770               	; 	#else
17771               	; 	nespw = 2			' NES/Coleco start on a 2-frame pass
17772               	; 	#endif
17773               	;
17774               	; 	' THE ONE AND ONLY BANK SWITCH THE PROGRAM EVER MAKES, and it happens
17775               	; 	' here, before the first frame.
17776               	; 	'
17777               	; 	' There are two data banks now. Bank 1 holds everything read while the
17778               	; 	' game is running -- sprite and store art, the templates, the lookup
17779               	; 	' tables -- and it is selected at the end of this routine and never
17780               	; 	' changed again, so every VARPTR/PEEK read in the program is reading a
17781               	; 	' page that is permanently mapped. That is the property that makes
17782               	; 	' banking safe here: a missed BANK SELECT returns bytes from the wrong
17783               	; 	' page with no error at build or run time, so the safest number of
17784               	; 	' switches during play is none.
17785               	; 	'
17786               	; 	' Bank 2 exists to hold data that is read ONCE, at setup, and never
17787               	; 	' again. The font is exactly that: two DEFINEs copy it into VRAM and
17788               	; 	' nothing reads font_bits or font_col for the rest of the run. So it can
17789               	; 	' live on a page that is mapped for the length of those two statements.
17790               	; 	'
17791               	; 	' IF THIS EVER FAILS IT FAILS LOUDLY. Select the wrong bank here and the
17792               	; 	' font is garbage on the title screen, immediately and unmistakably --
17793               	; 	' which is the same diagnostic the font used to provide by staying out of
17794               	; 	' the banks altogether, recovered for free.
17795               	;
17796               	; 	#if NES
17797               	; 	' THE FONT IS SENT WITH A COLOUR TABLE SO ITS PAPER IS NOT THE BACKDROP.
17798               	; 	'
17799               	; 	' With `#ncol = 0` the uploader puts ink `nink` on index 0 -- the UNIVERSAL
17800               	; 	' backdrop, black in the game -- so every character of text sat in its own
17801               	; 	' black box. The score line was a black strip across the top of a blue sky.
17802               	; 	'
17803               	; 	' Index 0 cannot be set per region (it is one colour for the whole screen),
17804               	; 	' so the only way to give text a ground is to put its PAPER on another
17805               	; 	' index, and paper is written into the second bitplane when the character
17806               	; 	' is uploaded. Hence a table: $B4 is light yellow on dark blue, which
17807               	; 	' nes_inkmap sends to index 3 and index 1.
17808               	; 	'
17809               	; 	' ONE FONT, NOT TWO. The first attempt at this made a SECOND copy of the
17810               	; 	' font at codes 197.. so the HUD could differ from the message boxes, and
17811               	; 	' that was both unnecessary and impossible: in game the HUD and the boxes
17812               	; 	' are the same text and want the same treatment, and 197..207 is only
17813               	; 	' ELEVEN free codes -- 208 up is the radar canvas (genart's SCAN_FIRST),
17814               	; 	' which scan_wipe rewrites as raw pattern memory every frame. The 59-char
17815               	; 	' copy appeared to upload and was scribbled over from its twelfth character
17816               	; 	' on. See checkpat.py, which now knows the canvas owns those codes.
17817               	; 	'
17818               	; 	' What index 1 IS comes from the attribute table, per region: the HUD row
17819               	; 	' is on P1 (dark blue, below) and the store is on P0.
17820               	; 	#nsrc = VARPTR font_bits(0)
17821               	; 	nchr = 32
17822               	; 	ncnt = 59
17823               	; 	ntab = 1
17824               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR, $B4 on every row of all 59 characters: light yellow
17825               	; 	' on dark blue, ink index 3 on paper index 1, and which colours those are
17826               	; 	' is then the attribute table's business, per region. It used to be a
17827               	; 	' 472-byte table of that one value (nes_fcol), kept because "ROM is not
17828               	; 	' the scarce budget" -- on the NES it is. A #ncol under $100 is the
17829               	; 	' colour byte itself (assets/nes_chr.asm, nes_chrinkrow).
17830               	; 	#ncol = $B4
17831               	; 	nink = 3
17832               	; 	GOSUB nes_def
17833               	; 	#else
17834               	; 	DEFINE CHAR 32,59,font_bits
17835 6BD2 0204  20 	li r4,32
     6BD4 0020     
17836 6BD6 0205  20 	li r5,15104
     6BD8 3B00     
17837 6BDA 0200  20 	li r0,cvb_FONT_BITS
     6BDC 304A     
17838 6BDE 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     6BE0 AE2A     
17839 6BE2 A1FA     	data define_char
17840               	; 	#endif
17841               	; 	' Without this the font keeps whatever CVBasic left in the colour table --
17842               	; 	' white on transparent -- which over a green store made the HUD unreadable.
17843               	; 	'
17844               	; 	' THIS WAS A VPOKE LOOP AND IT WAS THE SLOWEST THING IN THE BOOT: 1,416
17845               	; 	' writes of one constant, paced by 24 WAITs, which is what made the title
17846               	; 	' fill in visibly instead of appearing. DEFINE COLOR does the same job in a
17847               	; 	' single call with interrupts off, and it writes all three screen thirds
17848               	; 	' itself -- define_color always takes the LDIRVM3 triple-copy path, which is
17849               	; 	' also why esc_deck_col and floor0_colour below CANNOT use it: they patch
17850               	; 	' one third each.
17851               	; 	'
17852               	; 	' The table is 472 identical bytes (genfont.py emits it beside the glyphs).
17853               	; 	' It reads as waste and is not: it lives in the data bank, which had 860
17854               	; 	' bytes spare, while the loop it replaced cost time in the one place the
17855               	; 	' player is made to wait.
17856               	; 	#if NES
17857               	; 	' no colour table on this machine -- see nes_setup
17858               	; 	#else

17869               	; 	' 16x16 so the game's name reads as a name rather than as a line of body

17871               	; 	' it could not go there; it did not need to, because it is read ONCE, by

18096               	; 		jarc(ji) = PEEK(#jaa)

18099               	;
18100               	; 	' THE JUMP ARC IS A TABLE, not integration. That makes the 14 px apex a
18101               	; 	' property of the data rather than of a fixed-point velocity that has to
18102               	; 	' be tuned, and it keeps every comparison in the jump 8-bit and unsigned.
18103               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a depends on the apex being exactly 14.
18104               	; 	'
18105               	; 	' THIRTY FRAMES WITH NINE OF THEM AT THE APEX. The first version was 24
18106               	; 	' frames that touched 14 for only four, which made every jump a timing
18107               	; 	' test rather than a decision -- you had to leave the ground on exactly
18108               	; 	' the right frame or clip the thing you were jumping. Widening the
18109               	; 	' plateau rather than raising the apex keeps the ball arithmetic in

18148               	;
18149               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
18150               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
18151               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
18152               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
18153               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
18154               	; 	'
18155               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
18156               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
18157               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
18158               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
18159               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
18160               	; 	'
18161               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
18162               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
18163               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
18164               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
18165               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
18166               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
18167               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
18168               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
18169               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air
18170               	; 	' belonging to the floor BELOW it (see SLAB), which is right for three of
18171               	; 	' the four bars and wrong for the last one: below floor 0 there is no
18172               	; 	' floor, only the scanner, and the green read as a strip of shop with
18173               	; 	' nothing in it.
18174               	; 	'
18175               	; 	' NO NEW CHARACTER IS NEEDED, BECAUSE THE COLOUR TABLE HAS THREE COPIES
18176               	; 	' -- one per eight screen rows -- and the bands land such that each bar
18177               	; 	' sits in a different third:
18178               	; 	'
18179               	; 	'     band 0 roof   rows  1-5    bar row  5   third 0
18180               	; 	'     band 1        rows  6-10   bar row 10   third 1
18181               	; 	'     band 2        rows 11-15   bar row 15   third 1
18182               	; 	'     band 3 GROUND rows 16-20   bar row 20   third 2
18183               	; 	'
18184               	; 	' so recolouring SLAB in third 2 alone reaches the ground floor's bar and
18185               	; 	' nothing else. The same third also holds the scanner, but the scanner
18186               	; 	' does not use these characters. This is the same mechanism that once hid
18187               	; 	' a bug for months (CLAUDE.md 3A, the blanked-in-one-third note) used
18188               	; 	' deliberately for once.
18189               	; 	'
18190               	; 	' Only the three bottom lines change, and only their BACKGROUND: SLAB has
18191               	; 	' no ink there and SLABE's brick keeps its grey.
18192               	;

21141               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- LZSS (TI)
21142               	; 	' THE DECODER for assets/lzss.py's format: a flag byte governs eight items,
21143               	; 	' least significant bit first; 1 = a literal byte, 0 = a two-byte match,
21144               	; 	' big-endian (offset << 4 | length - 3), offset 1..4095 back into the
21145               	; 	' output. #lzs = the compressed stream, #lzd = the RAM destination, #lzn =
21146               	; 	' the output length (it stops there, so a stream's padding is never read).
21147               	; 	' R1-R9 only: R10 is CVBasic's stack pointer and R11 its return link.
21148               	; 	' It lives in BANK 1 with its stream, which must be selected (power-on
21149               	; 	' selects it before calling lz_probe), and needs no fixed-area room.
